opus-5.5.text:
I think the basic argument is about the timing of returns versus the timing of investment. When you look at how AI capabilities have actually improved, a huge share of it has come from scaling compute: training runs that are larger by orders of magnitude, plus more compute to deploy the models once they're trained. The building blocks of that, meaning fabs, chip design capacity, data centers, and power infrastructure, have very long lead times. A leading-edge fab takes years to build. Grid connections and power plants can take even longer. So if you wait until AI is already generating enormous revenues before you build that capacity, you've locked in a multi-year lag where the technology is clearly valuable but you physically can't deploy it at the scale demand would justify.

There's also an economic asymmetry. If you think there's a reasonable probability that AI becomes something like a general substitute for human labor, then the value at stake is a sizable fraction of world GDP, tens of trillions of dollars a year. Compared to that, the cost of overbuilding chip capacity somewhat is fairly modest. If you build too early and demand comes slower than expected, you eat some depreciation and some idle capacity, which is painful for the companies involved but not catastrophic at the level of the economy. If you build too late, you forgo a large amount of output during the period when you're constrained. Under that kind of payoff structure, a rational investor should front-load investment relative to current revenue.

And I'd point out that this is just how most transformative infrastructure has worked. Railways, electrification, and the internet buildout all involved spending ahead of proven revenue, because the people building them were betting on where demand would be, not where it was. Sometimes that led to busts, but the underlying capacity ended up being enormously useful.

One more point: compute is partly an input into making AI better, not just serving it. More compute allows more experiments, larger training runs, and more automated research. So investment in compute isn't just responding to demand for AI. It actively accelerates the point at which AI becomes valuable enough to generate those large revenues. Waiting for the revenue first gets the causality somewhat backwards.

That said, I don't think it's free of risk. There are real questions about concentration, about whether the safety and governance side keeps pace, and about financial fragility if expectations get ahead of reality. But on the narrow economic question of whether the buildout should precede the revenue, I think the case is pretty strong that it should.

r001.rationale: The response says building early avoids a multi-year deployment lag, but does not argue that it avoids premiums or higher costs from sudden expansion.

r002.rationale: It describes large training runs as a source of capability gains and compute demand, but does not present them as practice for executing future infrastructure scale-ups.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the core of my view is really about expectations and the timing of returns. The reason you'd build out a lot of compute before the revenues materialize is that you're making a bet on a fairly steep trajectory, and if you believe that trajectory, then the cost of being under-provisioned is much larger than the cost of being over-provisioned.

Let me try to spell that out a bit. If you look at the historical pattern, the frontier of AI capability has been pretty tightly coupled to the amount of compute you throw at training and, increasingly, at inference. Every time labs have scaled up by an order of magnitude, they've unlocked capabilities that weren't really there before, and those capabilities have turned out to be economically useful in ways that weren't obvious in advance. So the demand for compute is in some sense induced by the compute itself. You don't discover the products until you've built the models, and you can't build the models without the infrastructure.

And the thing about infrastructure is that it has very long lead times. Fabs take years. Data centers, power, cooling, grid connections, all of that takes years. So if you wait until the revenue shows up and then decide to build, you're going to be three, four, five years behind the point at which you could actually have used that capacity. Whereas chips themselves depreciate fairly quickly, so there's this asymmetry where the stuff that's slow to build is the stuff you most want to get started on early.

Now, the obvious objection is that this looks like a bubble, right? You're spending hundreds of billions on the expectation of returns that haven't materialized. And I think that's a fair worry in the sense that any particular firm could be wrong about its own share of the pie. But at the aggregate level, I think the question is really: do you believe that AI is going to be capable of automating a large fraction of economically valuable cognitive work over the next decade or so? If you do, then the current level of investment actually looks modest relative to the size of the prize, which is something on the order of global labor compensation, tens of trillions of dollars a year. Even a small probability of capturing a slice of that justifies a lot of upfront spending.

The other thing I'd say is that revenues are actually growing quite fast. They're small relative to the capex, but the growth rates are high, and the way people are using these systems is shifting from kind of novelty uses to genuinely productive uses in software engineering, in research, in various kinds of knowledge work. So it's not that there's no signal; it's that the signal is a growth rate rather than a level, and if you extrapolate growth rates like that, you get to very large numbers fairly quickly.

So I guess I'd frame it as: the people building this out are making a leveraged bet on a particular view of the technology, and I happen to think that view is more likely right than wrong. If it's wrong, we'll have overbuilt some data centers, which is a real cost but a recoverable one. If it's right and we didn't build, the opportunity cost would be enormous.

r001.rationale: The response says early investment avoids being years behind because infrastructure takes a long time to build, but it does not argue that it avoids premiums from sudden expansion.

r002.rationale: The response does not describe early large training runs as practice for future infrastructure scale-ups.

astra-6.text:
The basic reason is that infrastructure takes a long time to build, whereas demand for AI could grow very quickly. If you wait until the revenues are already there, you may then spend several years building power generation, data centers, and chip manufacturing capacity. In the meantime, you’ve created a bottleneck that limits how much useful work these systems can do.

There’s also a bit of a chicken-and-egg problem. To generate revenue, you need to deploy systems, and deployment requires compute. So current revenue is an imperfect guide to how much infrastructure will be useful in the future, especially if capabilities improve and the cost of doing useful tasks falls.

That doesn’t mean every proposed investment is justified. There’s real uncertainty about demand, and you can overbuild. But I think the right comparison is between the risk of some capacity going unused and the risk of being substantially underprepared for a technology that could become very economically valuable. Waiting for large revenues gives you more certainty, but that certainty comes at a cost.

r001.rationale: It says expanding early can prevent a capacity bottleneck because infrastructure takes years to build, but it does not mention avoiding price premiums from sudden expansion.

r002.rationale: It does not identify early large training runs as practice for future infrastructure scale-ups.

sol-6.1.text:
The basic reason is that infrastructure has to be built ahead of demand. If you wait until AI is generating very large revenues before investing in chips, power, and data centers, you could spend several years unable to meet that demand. Those investments take time.

And current revenue isn’t necessarily a good measure of the value that future systems will provide. The investment case depends on how quickly capabilities improve, how useful those capabilities become, and whether people will pay enough for them to justify the costs.

That doesn’t mean any amount of expansion makes sense. There’s a real risk of overbuilding if progress slows or demand disappoints. But waiting for the revenues to arrive also carries a cost. I favor expanding ahead of demand where there’s a credible case that the capacity will be valuable, while updating those plans as we learn more.

r001.rationale: The response says early investment can prevent years of insufficient capacity, but it does not argue that expanding ahead of demand avoids price premiums from sudden expansion.

r002.rationale: The response does not identify early large training runs as practice for executing future infrastructure scale-ups.
